section.heading: 2.2 The Inverse of a Matrix
section.paragraph: Matrix algebra provides tools for manipulating matrix equations and creating various useful formulas in ways similar to doing ordinary algebra with real numbers. This section investigates the matrix analogue of the reciprocal, or multiplicative inverse, of a nonzero number.
Recall that the multiplicative inverse of a number such as $$5$$ is $$1/5$$ or $$5^{- 1}$$ . This inverse satisfies the equations
$$5^{- 1} \left(\right. 5 \left.\right) = 1 \text{and} 5 \left(\right. 5^{- 1} \left.\right) = 1$$

The matrix generalization requires both equations and avoids the slanted-line notation (for division) because matrix multiplication is not commutative. Furthermore, a full generalization is possible only if the matrices involved are square.1
An $$n \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ is said to be invertible if there is an $$n \times n$$ matrix $$C$$ such that
$$C A = I \text{and} A C = I$$

where $$I = I_{n}$$ , the $$n \times n$$ identity matrix. In this case, $$C$$ is an inverse of $$A$$ . In fact, $$C$$ is uniquely determined by $$A$$ , because if $$B$$ were another inverse of $$A$$ , then $$B = BI = B(A C) = (B A)C = IC = C$$ . This unique inverse is denoted by $$A^{- 1}$$ , so that
$$\boxed{A^{- 1} A = I \text{and} A A^{- 1} = I}$$
A matrix that is not invertible is sometimes called a singular matrix, and an invertible matrix is called a nonsingular matrix.
Here is a simple formula for the inverse of a $$2 \times 2$$ matrix, along with a test to tell if the inverse exists.

note.title: Theorem 4
note.heading: Theorem 4
note.paragraph: Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$$ . If $$ad - bc \neq 0$$ , then $$A$$ is invertible and
$$A^{- 1} = \frac{1}{a d - b c} \begin{bmatrix} d & - b \\ - c & a \end{bmatrix}$$
If $$ad - bc = 0$$ , then $$A$$ is not invertible.

section.paragraph: The simple proof of Theorem 4 is outlined in Exercises 35 and 36. The quantity $$ad - bc$$ is called the determinant of $$A$$ , and we write
$$\boxed{\det A = a d - b c}$$
Theorem 4 says that a $$2 \times 2$$ matrix $$A$$ is invertible if and only if $$\text{det} A \neq 0$$ .﻿

Invertible matrices are indispensable in linear algebra—mainly for algebraic calculations and formula derivations, as in the next theorem. There are also occasions when an inverse matrix provides insight into a mathematical model of a real-life situation, as in Example 3.

note.title: Theorem 5
note.heading: Theorem 5
note.paragraph: If $$A$$ is an invertible $$n \times n$$ matrix, then for each $$\textbf{b}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ has the unique solution $$\textbf{x} = A^{- 1}\textbf{b}$$ .﻿

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Take any $$\textbf{b}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . A solution exists because if $$A^{- 1}\textbf{b}$$ is substituted for $$\textbf{x}$$ , then $$A\textbf{x} = A(A^{- 1}\textbf{b}) = (AA^{- 1})\textbf{b} = I\textbf{b} = \textbf{b}$$ . So $$A^{- 1}\textbf{b}$$ is a solution. To prove that the solution is unique, show that if $$\textbf{u}$$ is any solution, then $$\textbf{u}$$ , in fact, must be $$A^{- 1}\textbf{b}$$ . Indeed, if $$A\textbf{u} = \textbf{b}$$ , we can multiply both sides by $$A^{- 1}$$ and obtain
$$A^{- 1} A \textbf{u} = A^{- 1} \textbf{b} , I \textbf{u} = A^{- 1} \textbf{b} , \text{and} \textbf{u} = A^{- 1} \textbf{b}$$

To study the stiffness matrix $$D^{- 1}$$ , observe that the equation $$\textbf{f} = D^{- 1}\textbf{y}$$ computes a force vector $$\textbf{f}$$ when a deflection vector $$\textbf{y}$$ is given. Write

Now interpret $$\textbf{e}_{1}$$ as a deflection vector. Then $$D^{- 1}\textbf{e}_{1}$$ lists the forces that create the deflection. That is, the first column of $$D^{- 1}$$ lists the forces that must be applied at the three points to produce a unit deflection at point $$1$$ and zero deflections at the other points. Similarly, columns $$2$$ and $$3$$ of $$D^{- 1}$$ list the forces required to produce unit deflections at points $$2$$ and $$3$$ , respectively. In each column, one or two of the forces must be negative (point upward) to produce a unit deflection at the desired point and zero deflections at the other two points. If the flexibility is measured, for example, in inches of deflection per pound of load, then the stiffness matrix entries are given in pounds of load per inch of deflection.

section.paragraph: The formula in Theorem 5 is seldom used to solve an equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ numerically because row reduction of $$\begin{bmatrix} A & \textbf{b} \end{bmatrix}$$ is nearly always faster. (Row reduction is usually more accurate, too, when computations involve rounding off numbers.) One possible exception is the $$2 \times 2$$ case. In this case, mental computations to solve $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ are sometimes easier using the formula for $$A^{- 1}$$ , as in the next example.

section.paragraph: The next theorem provides three useful facts about invertible matrices.

list.item: If $$A$$ is an invertible matrix, then $$A^{- 1}$$ is invertible and $$\left(A^{- 1}\right)^{- 1} = A$$

If $$A$$ and $$B$$ are $$n \times n$$ invertible matrices, then so is $$A B$$ , and the inverse of $$A B$$ is the product of the inverses of $$A$$ and $$B$$ in the reverse order. That is, $$\left(A B\right)^{- 1} = B^{- 1} A^{- 1}$$
If $$A$$ is an invertible matrix, then so is $$A^{T}$$ , and the inverse of $$A^{T}$$ is the transpose of $$A^{- 1}$$ . That is, $$\left(( A^{T} )\right)^{- 1} = \left(( A^{- 1} )\right)^{T}$$

In fact, these equations are satisfied with $$A$$ in place of $$C$$ . Hence $$A^{- 1}$$ is invertible, and $$A$$ is its inverse. Next, to prove statement (b), compute:
$$\left(\right. A B \left.\right) \left(\right. B^{- 1} A^{- 1} \left.\right) = A \left(\right. B B^{- 1} \left.\right) A^{- 1} = A I A^{- 1} = A A^{- 1} = I$$

A similar calculation shows that $$(B^{- 1}A^{- 1})(A B) = I$$ . For statement (c), use Theorem 3(d), read from right to left, $$(A^{- 1})^{T}A^{T} = (AA^{- 1})^{T} = I^{T} = I$$ . Similarly, $$A^{T}(A^{- 1})^{T} = I^{T} = I$$ . Hence $$A^{T}$$ is invertible, and its inverse is $$(A^{- 1})^{T}$$ .﻿

Remark: Part (b) illustrates the important role that definitions play in proofs. The theorem claims that $$B^{- 1}A^{- 1}$$ is the inverse of $$AB$$ . The proof establishes this by showing that $$B^{- 1}A^{- 1}$$ satisfies the definition of what it means to be the inverse of $$AB$$ . Now, the inverse of $$AB$$ is a matrix that when multiplied on the left (or right) by $$AB$$ , the product is the identity matrix $$I$$ . So the proof consists of showing that $$B^{- 1}A^{- 1}$$ has this property.

note.paragraph: The product of $$n \times n$$ invertible matrices is invertible, and the inverse is the product of their inverses in the reverse order.

section.paragraph: There is an important connection between invertible matrices and row operations that leads to a method for computing inverses. As we shall see, an invertible matrix $$A$$ is row equivalent to an identity matrix, and we can find $$A^{- 1}$$ by watching the row reduction of $$A$$ to $$I$$ .
section.heading: Elementary Matrices
section.paragraph: An elementary matrix is one that is obtained by performing a single elementary row operation on an identity matrix. The next example illustrates the three kinds of elementary matrices.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: $$E_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ - 4 & 0 & 1\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} , E_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} , E_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} , A = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}a & b & c \\ d & e & f \\ g & h & i\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$
Compute $$E_{1}A$$ , $$E_{2}A$$ , and $$E_{3}A$$ , and describe how these products can be obtained by elementary row operations on $$A$$ .﻿
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: $$E_{1} A = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}a & b & c \\ d & e & f \\ g - 4 a & h - 4 b & i - 4 c\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} , E_{2} A = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}d & e & f \\ a & b & c \\ g & h & i\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} , E_{3} A = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}a & b & c \\ d & e & f \\ 5 g & 5 h & 5 i\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} .$$

Addition of $$- 4$$ times row $$1$$ of $$A$$ to row $$3$$ produces $$E_{1}A$$ . (This is a row replacement operation.) An interchange of rows $$1$$ and $$2$$ of $$A$$ produces $$E_{2}A$$ , and multiplication of row $$3$$ of $$A$$ by $$5$$ produces $$E_{3}A$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: Left-multiplication (that is, multiplication on the left) by $$E_{1}$$ in Example 5 has the same effect on any $$3 \times n$$ matrix. It adds $$- 4$$ times row $$1$$ to row $$3$$ . In particular, since $$E_{1} \cdot I = E_{1}$$ , we see that $$E_{1}$$ itself is produced by this same row operation on the identity. Thus Example 5 illustrates the following general fact about elementary matrices. See Exercises 37 and 38.

note.paragraph: If an elementary row operation is performed on an $$m \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ , the resulting matrix can be written as $$E A$$ , where the $$m \times m$$ matrix $$E$$ is created by performing the same row operation on $$I_{m}$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: Since row operations are reversible, as shown in Section 1.1, elementary matrices are invertible, for if $$E$$ is produced by a row operation on $$I$$ , then there is another row operation of the same type that changes $$E$$ back into $$I$$ . Hence there is an elementary matrix $$F$$ such that $$F E = I$$ . Since $$E$$ and $$F$$ correspond to reverse operations, $$E F = I$$ , too.

note.paragraph: Each elementary matrix $$E$$ is invertible. The inverse of $$E$$ is the elementary matrix of the same type that transforms $$E$$ back into $$I$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: The following theorem provides the best way to “visualize” an invertible matrix, and the theorem leads immediately to a method for finding the inverse of a matrix.

note.title: Theorem 7
note.heading: Theorem 7
note.paragraph: An $$n \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ is invertible if and only if $$A$$ is row equivalent to $$I_{n}$$ , and in this case, any sequence of elementary row operations that reduces $$A$$ to $$I_{n}$$ also transforms $$I_{n}$$ into $$A^{- 1}$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: Remark: The comment on the proof of Theorem 11 in Chapter 1 noted that “ $$P$$ if and only if $$Q$$ ” is equivalent to two statements: (1) “If $$P$$ then $$Q$$ ” and (2) “If $$Q$$ then $$P$$ .” The second statement is called the converse of the first and explains the use of the word conversely in the second paragraph of this proof.
section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Suppose that $$A$$ is invertible. Then, since the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ has a solution for each $$\textbf{b}$$ (Theorem 5), $$A$$ has a pivot position in every row (Theorem 4 in Section 1.4). Because $$A$$ is square, the $$n$$ pivot positions must be on the diagonal, which implies that the reduced echelon form of $$A$$ is $$I_{n}$$ . That is, $$A \sim I_{n}$$ .﻿

Now suppose, conversely, that $$A \sim I_{n}$$ . Then, since each step of the row reduction of $$A$$ corresponds to left-multiplication by an elementary matrix, there exist elementary matrices $$E_{1},\ldots,E_{p}$$ such that
$$A sim E_{1} A sim E_{2} \left(\right. E_{1} A \left.\right) sim \hdots sim E_{p} \left(\right. E_{p - 1} \hdots E_{1} A \left.\right) = I_{n}$$
That is,
$$E_{p} \hdots E_{1} A = I_{n}$$
Since the product $$E_{p}\cdots E_{1}$$ of invertible matrices is invertible, (1) leads to

$$\left(\right. E_{p} \hdots E_{1} \left.\right)^{- 1} \left(\right. E_{p} \hdots E_{1} \left.\right) A & = \left(\right. E_{p} \hdots E_{1} \left.\right)^{- 1} I_{n} A & = \left(\right. E_{p} \hdots E_{1} \left.\right)^{- 1}$$
Thus $$A$$ is invertible, as it is the inverse of an invertible matrix (Theorem 6). Also,
$$A^{- 1} = \begin{bmatrix} \left(\right. E_{p} \hdots E_{1} \left.\right)^{- 1} \end{bmatrix}^{- 1} = E_{p} \hdots E_{1}$$

Then $$A^{- 1} = E_{p}\cdots E_{1}I_{n}$$ , which says that $$A^{- 1}$$ results from applying $$E_{1},\ldots,E_{p}$$ successively to $$I_{n}$$ . This is the same sequence in (1) that reduced $$A$$ to $$I_{n}$$ .﻿
section.heading: An Algorithm for Finding A−1
section.paragraph: If we place $$A$$ and $$I$$ side by side to form an augmented matrix $$\begin{bmatrix} A & I \end{bmatrix}$$ , then row operations on this matrix produce identical operations on $$A$$ and on $$I$$ . By Theorem 7, either there are row operations that transform $$A$$ to $$I_{n}$$ and $$I_{n}$$ to $$A^{- 1}$$ or else $$A$$ is not invertible.

note.title: Algorithm for Finding A−1
note.heading: Algorithm for Finding A−1
note.paragraph: Row reduce the augmented matrix $$\begin{bmatrix} A & I \end{bmatrix}$$ . If $$A$$ is row equivalent to $$I$$ , then $$\begin{bmatrix} A & I \end{bmatrix}$$ is row equivalent to $$\begin{bmatrix} I & A^{- 1} \end{bmatrix}$$ . Otherwise, $$A$$ does not have an inverse.

section.heading: Another View of Matrix Inversion
section.paragraph: Denote the columns of $$I_{n}$$ by $$\textbf{e}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{e}_{n}$$ . Then row reduction of $$\begin{bmatrix} A & I \end{bmatrix}$$ to $$\begin{bmatrix} I & A^{- 1} \end{bmatrix}$$ can be viewed as the simultaneous solution of the $$n$$ systems
$$A \textbf{x} = \textbf{e}_{1} , A \textbf{x} = \textbf{e}_{2} , \ldots , A \textbf{x} = \textbf{e}_{n}$$

where the “augmented columns” of these systems have all been placed next to $$A$$ to form $$\begin{bmatrix} A & \textbf{e}_{1} & \textbf{e}_{2} & \cdots & \textbf{e}_{n} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} A & I \end{bmatrix}$$ . The equation $$AA^{- 1} = I$$ and the definition of matrix multiplication show that the columns of $$A^{- 1}$$ are precisely the solutions of the systems in (2). This observation is useful because some applied problems may require finding only one or two columns of $$A^{- 1}$$ . In this case, only the corresponding systems in (2) need to be solved.

note.title: Numerical Note
note.heading: Numerical Note
note.paragraph: In practical work, $$A^{- 1}$$ is seldom computed, unless the entries of $$A^{- 1}$$ are needed. Computing both $$A^{- 1}$$ and $$A^{- 1}\textbf{b}$$ takes about three times as many arithmetic operations as solving $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ by row reduction, and row reduction may be more accurate.
